sandhi.rule: महत् becomes महा- as the first member of a karmadhāraya (described in words; no sūtra from the list applies)
sandhi.note: The same replacement gives महामाया, महामेधा, महास्मृतिः.

samasa.sense: at the end you take the form of dissolution — completing creation and preservation of 1.76
the power of understanding and retaining
memory, and also the remembered tradition (smṛti)

morph.note: The suffix -मय (mayaṭ) means ‘consisting of’; feminine जगन्मयी, vocative जगन्मये (ī shortened to e in the vocative of feminines in -ī).
संहृति ‘drawing together, withdrawal’ is सम् + √हृ + ktin: the dissolution pictured as the world gathered back in.

mantras.anvaya: जगन्मये, तथा अस्य जगतः अन्ते (त्वं) संहृतिरूपा। (त्वं) महाविद्या, महामाया, महामेधा, महास्मृतिः, …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the series of 1.76 (सृष्टिरूपा … स्थितिरूपा … संहृतिरूपा); the second begins a list of nominatives predicated of the Goddess, continued in 1.78.
mantras.lit: so too, at the end of this world, the form of dissolution, O you who consist of the world. (You are) the great knowledge, the great illusion, the great intelligence, the great memory,
mantras.tr: and at the end of this world, O you whose being is the world, you are its dissolution. You are the Great Knowledge and the Great Illusion, the Great Intelligence and the Great Memory,

comm.t: The triad of 1.76 is completed: at the world’s end she takes the form of its dissolution. Then begins a litany of ‘great’ names — knowledge, illusion, intelligence, memory. Two printing errors of the digital text are corrected in this verse (सिंहृति → संहृति, महास्मृतः → महास्मृतिः), both with the independent witnesses; see corrections.json.

Mahāvidyā and Mahāmāyā stand side by side, as liberation and bondage did in 1.57–58: the Goddess is both the knowledge that frees and the illusion that binds. ‘Great’ marks each as her cosmic form, not a human faculty.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 584, महाविद्या, and 215, महामाया, and the simple forms 538, मेधा, and 540, स्मृतिः.

samasa.sense: she who is the great power of delusion
samasa.alt: The feminine ending shows the compound describes the Goddess; it may also be read as a karmadhāraya personified in the feminine (‘the Great Delusion’). The sense is the same.

samasa.sense: she whose power includes even the demonic; or, in the old sense of asura ‘mighty lord’, the great mighty one
samasa.alt: The witnesses GRETIL and Freund read महेश्वरी, ‘great sovereign’ (महती चासौ ईश्वरी च, karmadhāraya). The Gita Press reading is kept; see flags.

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī (upapada-type) tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (गुणत्रय)
samasa.literal: manifester of the triad of guṇas
samasa.sense: she who unfolds sattva, rajas and tamas

morph.note: The feminine of the honorific भवत् (‘Your Ladyship’); in Brahmā’s hymn it alternates with the familiar त्वम्, which follows in the next line.
विभाविन् is an agent noun from the causative of वि + √भू (‘cause to appear distinctly’) with the kṛt affix -in; feminine -ī.

mantras.anvaya: भवती च महामोहा, महादेवी, महासुरी। त्वं च सर्वस्य गुणत्रयविभाविनी प्रकृतिः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The list of 1.77 continues with भवती as its expressed subject; a second clause names her as Prakṛti, with सर्वस्य and an epithet.
mantras.lit: And Your Ladyship (is) the great delusion, the great Goddess, the great Asurī; and you are the primal nature of all, who brings forth the three guṇas.
mantras.tr: and Great Delusion, Great Goddess and mighty Asurī. You are the primal Nature of all things, unfolding the three qualities.

comm.t: The litany continues: she is the great delusion as well as the great knowledge of 1.77, the great Goddess, and — in the Gita Press reading — the great Asurī. She is also Prakṛti, the material source of everything, from which the three guṇas unfold.

The Sāṃkhya term prakṛti is taken over: matter and its three qualities (sattva, rajas, tamas) are not an inert principle opposed to spirit but the Goddess herself. The Gita Press pāṭha’s liturgical scheme, in which the three caritas are presided over by Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī and Mahāsarasvatī, is often explained through these guṇas; that scheme is tradition, not stated in this verse.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 209, महादेवी; 397, मूलप्रकृतिः; and 763, त्रिगुणात्मिका.

flags.uncertain: Variant reading (corrections.json, status ‘Textual Verification Required’): the Gita Press text reads महादेवी महासुरी; GRETIL (MkP 81.58) and Freund read महादेवी महेश्वरी. The Gita Press reading is kept and analysed; it must be checked against the printed book.

samasa.sense: the night of dissolution brought by all-devouring Time
samasa.alt: Also a karmadhāraya, काली चासौ रात्रिः च ‘the black night’; Time-as-death fits the dissolution of 1.76–77 better.

samasa.sense: the great night of cosmic dissolution
the darkness of delusion in which beings are held
samasa.alt: Or a karmadhāraya of identity, मोहः एव रात्रिः ‘the night that is delusion’.

samasa.sense: intelligence known by its power to understand and to awaken

morph.note: Root-nouns in ī keep the visarga in the nominative singular (श्रीः, ह्रीः, धीः), unlike the derived feminines in ī (देवी, ईश्वरी) which have no ending.
Feminine of the adjective दारुण ‘harsh, dreadful’, agreeing with the feminine रात्रि compounds.

mantras.anvaya: (त्वं) कालरात्रिः, महारात्रिः, दारुणा मोहरात्रिः च। त्वं श्रीः, त्वम् ईश्वरी, त्वं ह्रीः, त्वं बोधलक्षणा बुद्धिः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three ‘night’ names with one adjective, then four identity statements each with त्वम्.
mantras.lit: (You are) the Night of Time, the Great Night, and the dreadful Night of Delusion. You are Śrī, you are the Sovereign, you are Modesty, you are Understanding, whose mark is awareness.
mantras.tr: You are the Night of Time, the Great Night, the terrible Night of Delusion. You are Fortune, you are the Sovereign, you are Modesty, you are Understanding, whose very mark is awakening.

comm.t: Brahmā names her as three nights — of Time, the Great Night, and the dreadful night of delusion — and then as Fortune, Sovereignty, Modesty and Understanding. The dark and the auspicious are named in one breath. बोध ‘awakening’ in the last word echoes the purpose of the hymn, the awakening (विबोधन) of Viṣṇu (1.70).

The three nights are commonly explained as nights of dissolution and of delusion, though explanations of each differ and the text does not define them. Kālarātri is also one of the nine Durgās: the Devī Kavaca recited before the Gita Press pāṭha names her seventh (सप्तमं कालरात्रीति). Here ह्री is the virtue of modesty, paired with लज्जा in 1.80, not a seed-syllable.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has 271, ईश्वरी, and describes her as 491, कालरात्र्यादिशक्त्यौघवृता, ‘surrounded by hosts of powers beginning with Kālarātri’ — there Kālarātri is one of her attendant powers, here one of her own names.
